video_title: Hedgeye Investing Summit Fall 2026 | Leyla Kunimoto, Founder, Accredited Investor Insights
gist: Leyla Kunimoto (Accredited Investor Insights) tells Keith McCullough that retail evergreen private credit (~$300B of a ~$2T market) is shrinking as 7 of the 9 largest non-traded BDCs/interval funds cap redemptions, while listed BDC siblings with heavily overlapping portfolios trade ~18-22% below NAV. She flags opaque Level 3 marks, PIK and ARR loans, floating-rate refinancing risk and insurers' private credit exposure as the risks to watch.

themes.theme: Private credit market size and retail outflows

insights.claim: Core private credit (middle-market direct lending to mostly PE-backed private companies) is about $2 trillion, with roughly two-thirds to three-quarters in institutional drawdown vehicles and about $300 billion in retail evergreen vehicles (interval funds, non-traded BDCs).
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Retail evergreen vehicles are a small but fragile slice of private credit where liquidity stress shows first.
insights.quote: what we think of as private credit is the middle market lending universe and that's about $2 trillion

insights.claim: Net assets in evergreen private credit vehicles fell from about $310 billion at end of Q1 to about $290 billion at end of Q2 2026 as retail money flows out.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Shrinking retail AUM signals sustained redemption pressure on non-traded vehicles and their sponsors.
insights.quote: So, it's shrinking

insights.claim: Of the nine largest non-traded BDCs and interval funds, only two are currently not capping redemptions.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Widespread gating means retail private credit investors are effectively trapped; negative read-through for alt-manager fundraising from the wealth channel.
insights.quote: out of the nine largest uh non-traded BDC's and interval funds, only two are currently not capped

insights.claim: Institutional fundraising into private credit drawdown vehicles was still going well as of June, diverging from the retail outflows from evergreen vehicles.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Stress is concentrated in the retail channel; institutional flows not yet confirming a broad private credit retreat.

insights.claim: Wealth-channel clients are pulling advisers toward private credit because of its ~9% headline yield, with clients asking why they are not in it.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Yield-chasing retail demand is the marginal buyer that sustained evergreen vehicle growth and is now reversing.
insights.quote: there's this wonderful thing that pays 9%. It's called private credit. Why am I not in it?

insights.claim: Non-traded BDC investors buy and redeem at NAV, with liquidity provided by the manager typically capped at 5% of shares per quarter; if 15% is requested, everyone is prorated to about a third and must re-queue.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Redemption mechanics create run dynamics: once a fund caps, advisers stop allocating new money, worsening the queue.
insights.quote: So a fund will redeem up to 5% typically up to 5% of shares per quarter.

insights.claim: Publicly listed BDCs (about 40 of them) are trading at an average discount of roughly 18-22% to NAV, i.e., the public market is skeptical of the NAVs that non-traded siblings transact at.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Listed BDC discounts are a real-time market signal that private credit marks are too high.

insights.claim: Investors in a major manager's non-traded BDC should consider redeeming at 100% of NAV and buying the very similar listed sibling at a ~22% discount with daily liquidity.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Clear relative-value trade: redeem non-traded at NAV, rotate into discounted listed BDCs (if redemptions are available).
insights.quote: why why don't we redeem me at NAV at NAV at 100%. and buy a very similar thing at a 22% discount in the public market

insights.claim: Every major asset manager runs both a listed BDC and a non-traded sibling (e.g., Blackstone's BXSL and its non-traded BDC) with massive portfolio overlap because they co-invest in the same deals; the listed vehicle carries slightly higher leverage. Anyone can verify this by feeding both schedules of investments into an LLM.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Overlap means listed BDC prices are a usable mark for the non-traded book; LLMs make this diligence cheap.
insights.quote: get the schedule of investments, throw it into your LLM from both vehicles and say, "Okay, what's the overlap?" And you'll be shocked by the amount of overlap.

insights.claim: Advisers are incentivized to place clients in non-traded BDCs rather than listed ones because the money is sticky and the lack of reported volatility is the main selling point.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Distribution incentives, not economics, explain retail flows; flows can reverse when the smooth-NAV story breaks.
insights.quote: the biggest selling point is the lack of volatility

insights.claim: Hedgeye is short a range of alternative asset managers and their BDCs, including Ares (and ARCC), Blackstone (and BXSL), and flags Blue Owl's OBDC, viewing both the managers' equity and their BDCs as shorts.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Hedgeye positioning: bearish alt managers and their listed credit vehicles into the credit cycle.
insights.quote: We're short everything from Aries to Blackstone, but they all have a BDC

insights.claim: Private credit loans are largely Level 3 assets valued by internal models with no observable inputs, so NAVs reflect manager assumptions rather than market prices.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: NAVs can lag reality materially; expect step-down marks when forced sales occur.
insights.quote: it's basically there's no observable inputs um valuations are determined based on internal models

insights.claim: The syndicated Medallia loan (a PE take-private of a large SaaS company that became impaired) was marked at materially divergent levels by different private credit holders for several quarters, undermining trust in marks.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Same-loan mark dispersion is evidence that private credit NAVs are discretionary.
insights.quote: there were a couple of quarters where marks on that one loan were diverging by a good margin

insights.claim: Non-traded private vehicles 'launder' volatility (citing Cliff Asness's paper) because they do not trade daily, which appeals to investors who want a smooth quarterly statement.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Smoothed returns understate risk; true volatility surfaces abruptly when liquidity is demanded.
insights.quote: There's a paper um by Cliff Asnases on volatility laundering

insights.claim: Some BDCs, public and private, have up to 20% of income as payment-in-kind (PIK), meaning income is recorded as loan balance growth rather than cash.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: High PIK share flags borrower stress and inflates reported income; screen BDCs for PIK %.
insights.quote: some BDC's both public and private have like up to 20% of borrowers who are not paying cash

insights.claim: Some BDCs disclose that around 22% of their book is ARR (annual recurring revenue) loans; ARR is a 'bogus' metric unrelated to profitability, and as a subscription business owner she gets loan pitches based on ARR at scary leverage levels.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: ARR lending to unprofitable software firms is a concentrated risk pocket, especially with AI pressure on SaaS.
insights.quote: ARR is a bogus number

insights.claim: Disclosure is limited to schedules of investments (e.g., ~375 positions with fair value and cost); investors cannot assess whether private borrowers can repay, and the lender's best case is just yield and par.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Asymmetric payoff with opaque credit quality means limited upside and unknowable downside for retail holders.
insights.quote: As an investor, from the outside, when I look at those vehicles, I can't tell if those borrowers are in a position to repay the loan.

insights.claim: Keith McCullough, recalling Carlyle Capital Corp in 2007, argues private credit marks resemble the 'fake marks' before 2008, and Dan Rasmussen calls the private credit yield a 'fool's yield'.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Historical analog: opaque-mark leveraged credit vehicles unraveled once counterparties marked positions.

insights.claim: A new SEC rule-amendment proposal for 'responsible retailization' of alternatives would expand access beyond net-worth tests (e.g., to CPAs and CFA charterholders) while making some vehicles less liquid; Kunimoto supports the reduced liquidity but worries about broader access.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Regulatory push widens the retail funnel for alt managers, a tailwind for flows but a rising consumer-protection risk.
insights.quote: They they call it responsible retailization

insights.claim: A structural reason private markets lack critical research is that these funds cannot be shorted, so there is no constituency paid to find problems.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Absence of short sellers means negative information arrives late and abruptly.
insights.quote: in the private markets there is no opportunity to short this stuff

themes.theme: Insurers as the private credit risk to watch

insights.claim: Insurers, not banks, are the key private credit risk to watch: they match long liabilities with long private assets (a point Apollo's Marc Rowan makes) but their balance sheets are highly opaque.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Life insurers with heavy private credit allocations are the potential contagion channel; scrutinize insurer financials.
insights.quote: Anybody who is who has a policy, a life policy, should go and pull up the financials of their insurance company.

insights.claim: A recently reported insurer with about 30% of its book in illiquid private credit is running into trouble with regulators in Florida and South Carolina.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Early sign of insurer stress tied to private credit concentration.
insights.quote: an insurer that has about 30% of its book is invested in private credit

themes.theme: Credit cycle catalysts: rates, refinancing, forced sales

insights.claim: About 99% of middle-market loans are floating rate, so every rate hike raises borrowers' interest burden, and an extra point can break a stretched business.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Rate path is a direct driver of private credit defaults.
insights.quote: 99% of middle market loans are floating rate

insights.claim: The 12-year private credit playbook of kicking the can via PE-to-PE sales and bigger refinancings breaks when acquisitions slow and borrowers must refinance at higher rates.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Slowing M&A/sponsor exits is a key leading indicator for private credit defaults.
insights.quote: that's been the playbook for the last 12 years

insights.claim: The key signal to watch is a large asset manager being forced to sell loans, revealing real transaction prices, though other holders need not mark down the same position.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Forced-sale prints would be the price-discovery event for private credit NAVs.
insights.quote: any very large asset manager that's going to be forced to sell the loans

insights.claim: Kunimoto does not see a clear systemic crisis from private credit, saying that if she did she would bet on it, but sees multiple interacting risk factors as a big question mark.
insights.speaker: Leyla Kunimoto
insights.so_what: Tempers the crash narrative: stress likely, systemic outcome uncertain.
insights.quote: I couldn't tell you whether it's going to cause a systemic problem. I just don't see it. If I saw it, I would be betting on it.

insights.claim: McCullough sees the economic and profit cycle peaks behind us, partly due to AI financing, with a slowdown and possible multiple rate hikes, which he calls the cocktail for every credit crisis he has risk-managed in 27 years.
insights.speaker: Keith McCullough
insights.so_what: Hedgeye macro view is bearish credit: slowdown plus higher rates.
insights.quote: that is the cocktail for every credit crisis I've ever had to risk manage going back 27 years
